title: Quantum Simulations of Two-Dimensional Non-Abelian Adjoint String Breaking
authors: Anthony N. Ciavarella, Roland de Putter, Ed Younis, Ermal Rrapaj
abstract: Quantum computers offer the potential to directly probe the dynamics of strongly coupled quantum field theories. As a step towards reaching this potential, local Krylov-based truncations of a pure SU(2) lattice gauge theory on a triangular lattice are constructed. Adjoint strings connected to dynamical gluons are constructed in this truncated theory, and the resonances dominating the long-term dynamics at a large value of the gauge coupling are determined. Local operators are constructed to identify string oscillations and breakings. This is used to perform a quantum simulation of adjoint string breaking on an $8\times8$ and $16\times8$-site lattice with ibm_boston using all 156 qubits. Quantitative agreement with tensor network simulations is obtained for circuits with 7,634 CZ gates with a two-qubit gate depth of 218. In this simulation, the rates of oscillations and glueball production are identified with a distinctly non-Abelian signature of the underlying gauge group.
summary: This work uses quantum computation to simulate the process of adjoint string breaking in a 2D SU(2) lattice gauge theory. By tracking string dynamics and measuring excitation rates, the authors confirm the non-Abelian nature of the underlying physics. The success demonstrates the feasibility of using quantum hardware to probe strongly coupled quantum field theories.
main_problem: The paper aims to simulate the complex dynamics of two-dimensional non-Abelian adjoint string breaking, moving beyond simpler quark-antiquark processes.
main_result: The quantum simulation achieved quantitative agreement with tensor network results, identifying a distinctly non-Abelian signature in the rates of string oscillations and glueball production.
method: The simulation uses local Krylov-based truncations of an SU(2) lattice gauge theory Hamiltonian, implemented on a quantum computer using circuits requiring thousands of CZ gates.
model_or_system: The system is an SU(2) lattice gauge theory on a triangular lattice in 2+1 dimensions. The Hamiltonian involves electric and magnetic energy terms, and the simulation focuses on creating and tracking adjoint strings using specific operators.
key_observables: String oscillation rates, glueball production rates, and the evolution of electric link energy.
important_parameters: The simulation was performed on an 8x8 and 16x8 lattice using 156 qubits, and the analysis focused on the large gauge coupling limit.
main_assumptions: The primary approximation is the use of a local Krylov-based truncation of the infinite-dimensional gauge degrees of freedom.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping of gauge fields onto qubits, the different configurations of adjoint strings (initial, breaking, oscillating), and the time evolution of electric link energy compared to tensor network results.
paper_structure: The paper details the construction of the truncated Hamiltonian, the methodology for creating adjoint strings, the simulation setup on quantum hardware, and the analysis of time evolution dynamics to distinguish non-Abelian signatures.
why_interesting: The direct application of quantum computation to simulate fundamental, strongly coupled quantum field theories like lattice gauge theories is a key area of quantum simulation, bridging condensed matter and high-energy physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Mapping of the SU(2) link gauge fields onto qubits placed at the center of each plaquette. The application of a plaquette operator flips a qubit from the 0 to 1 state. When neighboring qubits are in the 1 state, their shared link is unexcited.

FIG. 2. Different possible string configurations on the lattice. The left panel shows a single adjoint string. The top row on the right shows different ways this adjoint string can break on resonance, and the bottom row shows different ways that the string can oscillate. Note that there are other allowed final states given by rotations and reflections of these transitions. The probability for each configuration can be determined by measuring the pair of projectors shown on the lattice.

FIG. 3. Evolution of an adjoint string on an 8 × 8 lattice with g = 1.4. The upper plots show the error-mitigated results obtained from ibm boston and the lower plots show the results of an MPS simulation with maximum bond dimension 100. This evolution shows the breaking of the string and energy beginning to flow away from the initial string configuration.

FIG. 4. Probability of the adjoint string breaking and oscillating on an 8 × 8 lattice with g = 1.4. The dashed curves are MPS calculations with a max bond dimension of 100. The data points are the mitigated results from ibm boston. The solid lines are the time-dependent perturbation theory result computed in Appendix B. The left panel was computed using only two Trotter steps for each point and varying ∆t. The right panel was computed using Trotter step sizes of ∆t = 0.5, 0.75, 1. All simulations were performed using an even number of Trotter steps. For time slices sampled by multiple Trotter step sizes, only the results of the shallowest circuit are displayed.

FIG. 5. Evolution of the adjoint string on a 16×8 lattice. The Trotterized time evolution operator was synthesized on the dense encoding using BQSKit with g = 1.4 and ∆t = 0.5. The hardware results were computed on ibm boston without applying ODR.
